segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And a great sign appeared in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She was pregnant, and she was crying out in labor pains, in agony to give birth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And another sign appeared in heaven: look, a great red dragon with seven heads and ten horns, and on his heads seven diadems.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: His tail dragged down a third of the stars of the sky and threw them to the earth. And the dragon stood in front of the woman who was about to give birth, so that when she bore her child he might devour it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And she gave birth to a son, a male child, who is going to shepherd all the nations with an iron rod. And her child was snatched up to God and to his throne.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the woman fled into the wilderness, where she has a place prepared by God, so that there she would be nourished for one thousand two hundred sixty days.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And war broke out in heaven: Michael and his angels waged war on the dragon. The dragon waged war, and his angels with him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but he was not strong enough, and no place was found for them in heaven any longer.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the great dragon was thrown down, the ancient serpent, the one called Devil and Satan, the one who leads the whole world astray—he was thrown down to the earth, and his angels were thrown down with him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I heard a loud voice in heaven saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Now the salvation and the power and the kingdom of our God and the authority of his Christ have come, because the accuser of our brothers and sisters has been thrown down, the one who accuses them before our God day and night.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: And they conquered him because of the blood of the Lamb and because of the word of their testimony, and they did not love their lives even to the point of death.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Therefore rejoice, you heavens and you who dwell in them! Woe to the earth and the sea, because the devil has come down to you in great fury, knowing that he has only a short time.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And when the dragon saw that he had been thrown down to the earth, he pursued the woman who had given birth to the male child.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the woman was given the two wings of the great eagle, so that she might fly into the wilderness to her place, where she is nourished for a time and times and half a time, away from the presence of the serpent.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the serpent spewed water like a river from his mouth after the woman, so that the river would sweep her away.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the earth helped the woman: the earth opened its mouth and swallowed the river that the dragon had spewed from his mouth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the dragon was enraged at the woman and went off to make war on the rest of her offspring, those who keep the commandments of God and hold the testimony of Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he stood on the sand of the sea.

notes.note: The Greek word means both “heaven” and “sky”, and a first-century reader would not have needed to choose. The signs here could equally be read as appearing “in the sky”, where sun, moon and stars are. “Heaven” is kept because the scene continues from the heavenly temple of the preceding verse and leads into the war in heaven in verse 7; in verse 4 the same word is rendered “sky”.

In Greek this word meant a huge serpent, not the winged, fire-breathing creature of later European legend. The Greek Old Testament uses it for the sea monsters, such as Leviathan, that stand for chaos and for hostile empires like Egypt and Babylon. That is why verse 9 can call the same figure “the ancient serpent” without changing the image.

The Greek verb is the ordinary word for tending a flock, and was a common image for a king’s government. The phrase echoes Psalm 2:9 in its Greek form, where the Hebrew is usually read as “break”. Most translations render “rule”, and many scholars hold that with an iron rod the sense is stern or even destructive. “Shepherd” keeps the image a Greek reader would have heard.

The same Greek word is rendered “Gentiles” elsewhere in this translation where it means the non-Jewish peoples as distinct from Israel. Here, as generally in Revelation, the scope is all the peoples of the world, so “nations” is used.

notes.phrase: one thousand two hundred sixty days
notes.traditional: a thousand two hundred and threescore days
notes.note: This is the same period as the “time and times and half a time” of verse 14 (three and a half years) and the forty-two months mentioned elsewhere in Revelation. The figure comes from Daniel 7:25 and 12:7, where it marks a limited period during which God’s people are oppressed. How the period should be understood is disputed among interpreters.

notes.phrase: the ancient serpent, the one called Devil and Satan
notes.traditional: that old serpent, called the Devil, and Satan
notes.note: “Satan” is a Hebrew word meaning adversary or accuser, and the Greek word behind “Devil” means slanderer and is the Greek Old Testament’s usual translation of it. Both names prepare for the title “the accuser” in verse 10. “The ancient serpent” points back to the serpent of Genesis 3, whose enmity with the woman and her offspring (Genesis 3:15) is echoed in verse 17.

The Greek plural was the normal way to address or refer to a mixed group of fellow believers, women as well as men. “Brothers” alone now suggests men only, so the fuller phrase is used. Several modern translations do the same; others keep “brothers”.

The Greek verb is the ordinary word for winning a battle, a contest or a lawsuit. “Conquer” keeps the note of victory and the link with the promises “to the one who conquers” earlier in Revelation; “overcome” in modern English can suggest merely getting past a difficulty. The meaning is not disputed, and some major translations also use “conquer” here.

notes.traditional: by the blood of the Lamb
notes.note: The Greek construction normally gives the ground or reason for something rather than the instrument, so “because of” is the more exact rendering: the Lamb’s death and their testimony are the basis of the victory. Most translations have “by”, and some scholars think the distinction had weakened by this period. A few translations render as here.

The Greek can mean either the testimony that Jesus himself gave, which his followers hold fast, or their testimony about Jesus. Scholars are divided, and the translation leaves the phrase as open as the Greek. Some later manuscripts add “Christ”, which is why older English versions include it.

notes.traditional: And I stood upon the sand of the sea
notes.note: The earliest and best manuscripts read “he stood”, meaning the dragon, who takes his place on the shore as the beast rises from the sea in the next chapter. Many later manuscripts read “I stood”, making John the subject, and the King James Version follows them. Editions also differ on numbering: this sentence is variously counted as 12:18, the end of 12:17, or the beginning of 13:1.

candidates.reason: Translators split between “shepherd”, “tend” and “rule” (Revelation 2:27; 12:5; 19:15; John 21:16; Acts 20:28; 1 Peter 5:2), and the Psalm 2:9 echo is lost if the English varies.
The plural for fellow believers occurs throughout the New Testament and needs one policy on “brothers” versus “brothers and sisters”.
It recurs across the Gospels, the letters and Revelation, and translations waver between “deceive”, “lead astray” and “mislead”.
It is a key term in John and Revelation where “testimony” and “witness” compete, and the link with the verb and with μάρτυς should be handled consistently.
“Wilderness” and “desert” both appear in English versions, and the exodus echo depends on a consistent choice across the Gospels, Acts, Hebrews and Revelation.

warnings: Verse 11: ψυχή is not rendered with a register form (life; soul; person / people / everyone / human being; living being / living creature; mind; wholeheartedly; keep in suspense) and has no register-exception note.
